newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran bars state-funded papers from electioneering.
newsitem.headline: Iran bars state-funded papers from electioneering.

text.p: Iran's supreme leader has banned newspapers receiving state funds from providing publicity for a particular candidate in the run-up to presidential elections next month, Tehran newspapers said on Monday.

A statement by Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's office asked a body overseeing publicity by candidates in the May 23 election to remind publications which receive state funds that "they absolutely do not have the right to act as the organ of a particular wing or tendency", the newspapers said.

The move came after the daily Hamshahri, published by the Tehran municipality, was accused by backers of the conservative candidate, Parliament Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, of mostly covering one of his main rivals, Mohammad Khatami.
Tehran's mayor is a leading figure among centrists close to outgoing President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani who have backed Khatami, a former minister of culture and Islamic guidance.
The elections appeared to be shaping up as a two-horse race between Nateq-Nouri and Katami. Former intelligence minister Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshari is rated as another strong entrant.

The statement named Hamshahri as well as the newspaper Iran, which is published by the official news agency IRNA, and the dailies Kayhan and Ettelaat as publications that get state funds and should provide equal coverage to all candidates.
It said the rule applied to all publications receiving any public funds but did not say if that included those printed on subsidised newsprint -- which would cover most newspapers.

The daily Resalat, close to conservative Shi'ite Moslem clerics and bazaar merchants, has openly backed Nateq-Nouri while the newspaper Salam, published by radical Islamist intellectuals, has sided with Khatami.
Khatami's backers have accused the state radio and television of giving wide coverage to events involving Nateq-Nouri in his official capacity and ignoring their candidate.

A five-day candidate registration period ended on Monday. There was no official word on how many people had signed up, but the daily Jomhuri Eslami said the number was expected to reach 100. A dozen prominent figures have announced their intention to run.
Candidates will be screened in the next 10 days by the Guardian Council, a body of lawyers and clerics which in past elections disqualified all but a handful of those who signed up.
Rafsanjani is barred by the constitution from running for a third consecutive four-year term. His mandate ends on August 3.
Official campaigning will be allowed for 12 days, up to the day before the vote, after the list of approved candidates is annouced by the Guardian Council.
